subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Industry and Economic Activity Reading
subtitle: Reading practice on employment sectors, industrial change, supply chains and tourism.
description: A KS3 geography reading pack with short passages and comprehension questions. It supports revision of economic sectors, location factors, deindustrialisation, global supply chains, tourism impacts and sustainable tourism.

data.sourcePassage: Geographers divide jobs into four employment sectors. The primary sector collects or extracts raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. The secondary sector makes or processes goods, such as car manufacturing, food processing and construction. The tertiary sector provides services, including healthcare, education, transport, retail and tourism. The quaternary sector focuses on knowledge, research, data and high-level technology. These sectors are linked. A cotton T-shirt may involve a farmer growing cotton, a factory worker making fabric, a lorry driver moving boxes, a shop assistant selling clothes and a data analyst studying fashion trends. This shows why primary jobs are not automatically more important just because they come first.

data.sourcePassage: Employment structure is the percentage of workers in each economic sector. It often changes as countries develop, although the pattern is not exactly the same everywhere. In many lower-income economies, a large share of workers may be in primary jobs, especially farming. As a country industrialises, more workers may move into factories and construction. Later, secondary employment may decline because machines, robots and computer systems can do some tasks, and companies may move production to places with lower costs. At the same time, rising incomes increase demand for services such as healthcare, restaurants, retail, entertainment and tourism. In highly developed economies, education and technology can also increase quaternary jobs in research, design, finance, IT and science.

data.section: Industrial location and UK economic change
data.sourceTitle: From Heavy Industry to High-Tech Clusters
data.targetTitle: From Heavy Industry to High-Tech Clusters
data.sourcePassage: Industries do not locate randomly. Traditional heavy industries often needed raw materials, energy, water and transport. Steelworks, for example, needed iron ore, coal, water and rail links, so places such as Sheffield became strongly linked with steel. Coal shaped many South Wales communities because mines provided jobs and supported local shops and services. Later, many UK heavy industries declined due to cheaper imports, automation, global competition, changing energy use and older factories becoming less competitive. Modern high-tech industries often have different needs. Silicon Fen around Cambridge benefits from university research, skilled graduates, science parks, investment, good transport and links between businesses. This shows that location factors change over time, but businesses still need a good balance of cost and access.

data.sourcePassage: A supply chain is the full journey of a product from raw materials to the customer, and sometimes to repair, reuse, recycling or waste. Supply chains can be local, national or global. A cotton T-shirt, for example, may begin with cotton grown in India, the USA, China or Pakistan. The cotton may be cleaned and spun into yarn, then woven and sewn into a T-shirt in Bangladesh or Vietnam. It may then be packed, shipped through a container port and sold in a UK shop or online. Global supply chains create jobs and can make products cheaper, but they also raise questions. Workers may be paid low wages, pollution may be produced, goods may travel long distances, and the biggest profits may not stay in the place where the product is made.

data.sourcePassage: Tourism is a major form of economic activity. It can support hotels, restaurants, transport, museums, outdoor shops, guides and local services. In the Lake District, visitors are attracted by mountains, lakes, villages, wildlife, walking routes and literary links. Tourism brings jobs, income, improved facilities and conservation funding. However, it can also create problems. Large numbers of visitors can cause footpath erosion, traffic congestion, pressure on parking, disturbance to wildlife and higher house prices linked to second homes. Seasonality can mean businesses are busy in summer but quieter in winter. Sustainable tourism tries to balance the needs of tourists, local people, businesses and the environment. Management can include footpath repairs, visitor information, public transport schemes, parking controls, local guides, waste reduction and conservation work.
